To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the number of trials to the acquisition of key pecking increases from serial, to delay, to trace autoshaping in that order.

(a) autoshaping is a serial process, (b) the rate of acquisition increases as the interval between CS and US increases, (c) a change in illumination is a better conditioned stimulus than either a tone or houselight, (d) pecking is directed toward the CS early in acquisition, but not later, (e) pecking latency increases with extensive conditioning or with the use of diffuse CSs.

the number of trials to criterion in serial, delay, trace, and serial autoshaping procedures is a function of the duration of the conditioned stimulus, and that the conditioned stimulus is a determinant of the latency to pecking.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the acquisition of the keyp peck, which is a relatively simple operant response, by pigeons exposed to serial, trace, or delay autoshaping procedures, in which the conditioned stimulus was always a change in the response key.
the effects of the CS on the rate of acquisition, the latency of the response, and the direction of the response.
a comparison of the effects of different autoshaping procedures on the rate of acquisition and on the topography of the conditioned response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the more similar the CS and UCS, the more rapid the acquisition of the conditioned response, the more rapid and more directed the response, and the more rapid the development of the response to the CS.

pecking generated in the serial procedure was more likely to be directed at the conditioned stimulus, to be of shorter latency, and to occur earlier in the conditioning sequence, than pecking generated with the other three procedures.

the serial procedure is the best for the rapid acquisition of a key peck, that the 4-sec, 8- sec, 8- and 28- sec delay procedures are all effective, but that the 8-sec procedures are better than the 28-sec procedures, and that the trace procedures are less effective than the delay procedures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
serial, trace, and delay autoshaping procedures are all effective in producing key pecking.
pecking is more likely to be generated by serial procedures than by other procedures and that the CSs used in serial procedures are more effective than other CSs in eliciting pecking.
serial autoshaping procedures are more efficient than delay procedures, which are more efficient than trace procedures, in producing keypecking.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the serial procedure is the best of the three autoshaping procedures to use for the acquisition of a keypeck.
the serial procedure is the most effective procedure for establishing key pecking, but that this procedure does not produce pecking directed toward the CS, even after many sessions of training.
the trace and delay autoshaping procedures are not functionally equivalent.
